title: Trier Witch Persecutions: 365 Executed in One of the Earliest Mass Hunts
description: The Electorate of Trier saw one of the earliest and most intense large-scale witch persecutions in the German territories, lasting from approximately 1581 to 1593 under the authority of Archbishop Johann von Schöneberg and his suffragan bishop Peter Binsfeld. An estimated 365 people were burned, drawn from multiple villages that were reportedly almost entirely depopulated. The Trier persecution featured the characteristic dynamics of later German mass hunts: use of torture to extract names of accomplices, chain-reaction accusations spreading from one village to another, and the targeting of socially prominent figures as the panic intensified. Binsfeld published his Tractatus de Confessionibus Maleficorum et Sagarum (1589) partly to justify the Trier proceedings.
historiographical_note: The Trier persecution is documented by the contemporary account of the canon Dietrich Flade, who was himself eventually accused and executed. Brian Levack's The Witch-Hunt in Early Modern Europe (1987) uses Trier as a key example of the pan-German pattern of large persecutions clustered in the ecclesiastical territories of the Empire, where secular oversight by independent courts was absent.
source_method: Contemporary chronicle sources; Binsfeld, Tractatus (1589); secondary scholarship on German witch hunting
